title: How Cruise Ship Crews Eat, Shower & Sleep
asof: Figures as of 2026 · sources in description

shots.s: Above you, thousands of people are on vacation.
Pools. Waterslides. Endless buffets.
Now go down.
Below the passengers,
past the doors marked crew only,
is where you live.
No window.
A bunk bed, and up to three roommates.
Twelve-hour days are not unusual.
And no real day off, for months.
So how do you eat,
shower,
and sleep,
on a cruise ship?
Day one. You walk up the gangway.
Your new home is huge.
Take Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas.
Twenty decks.
About fifty-six hundred guests, two to a cabin.
Up to seventy-six hundred when it's packed.
And about twenty-three hundred and fifty crew.
That's one of you for every two or three guests.

d.small: crew to guests · Icon of the Seas

shots.s: Two worlds share one hull.
Guests get the top.
You get the bottom.
Crew areas sit on the lower decks,
behind doors guests can't open.
The main crew hallway runs from the front of the ship to the back.
Crews call it I-95, like the highway.
Your cabin, the crew mess and the laundry all branch off it.
Your cabin.
Most crew cabins have no window.
So you can't tell if it's day or night outside.
You share it with one, two, or even three people.
Senior crew may get a cabin to themselves.
You get a bunk.
A narrow mattress.
A couple of drawers underneath.
And a curtain.
That curtain is most of your privacy.
Your roommate might work nights.
You might work days.
And the ship is never quiet.
Engines hum. The floor vibrates.
Doors slam. Footsteps pass.
Alarms go off.
Your bathroom is part of the cabin.
Shower, toilet and sink.
You can almost reach all three without moving.
A curtain keeps the rest of the room dry.
Up to four people may share it.
So you learn to be quick.
On many ships, a central laundry washes your uniform.
Your own clothes?
Self-service crew laundry rooms.
Upstairs, guests have restaurants, cafés and a buffet.
Down here, you have the crew mess.
It's a canteen. Rows of tables. Serving lines.
Meals run at set times,
with different times for different shifts.
The crew comes from all over the world.
On some ships, the menu leans toward the crew's biggest nationalities.
Officers eat in their own, quieter mess.
And under maritime law, your food is free.
Want a drink after your shift?
The crew bar opens in the evening.
There's a little crew shop too.
No cash. It goes on your crew card.
Now the hard part.
You work every single day.
Your contract has no real days off.
Twelve-hour days are not unusual.
Some jobs run split shifts.
A few hours on, a break, then back on at night.
Galley crews can start before breakfast,
and finish after the late-night cleanup.
A deck officer might work four hours on, eight hours off.
So is there any limit?
Yes. The Maritime Labour Convention sets one.
At least ten hours of rest in any twenty-four.

d.small: minimum rest in any 24 hours · MLC 2006

shots.s: At least seventy-seven hours in any week.
Or, depending on the flag, no more than fourteen hours of work a day.
Rest can be split in two,
but one block has to be at least six hours.
And safety drills?
They're mandatory.
They often land in your rest time, or your port time.
So what do you do with a few free hours?
There's a crew gym.
There's a crew deck outside, often up near the bow.
There are crew parties at the bar.
Internet is often limited.
Newer ships are trying to do better.
For Icon of the Seas,
over a thousand crew members reviewed mockups of their spaces.
Their top requests?
More storage.
And more privacy.
Most contracts run somewhere between three and ten months.
Then you get one or two months at home.
Then you sign on again.
Same hallway. Maybe a new roommate.
Above you, thousands of new guests start their vacation.
Below them, you start day one again.
So, could you do six months below deck?
Off Limits Life.

d.tag: How people live where you can't go
